title: streaming-slab-scheduling-synthesis-oct-2027
content:
Purpose
---
This is a synthesis of a set of small-bench experiments exploring slab-based scheduling heuristics for streaming responses across different proxy topologies (inproc, sidecar, edge-proxy mesh). The goal: identify scheduling knobs that reduce p50/p95 token latency under mixed workloads while not increasing CPU/NET cost excessively.

Quick summary (TL;DR)
- Small slabs (256B-1KB) reduce head-of-line effects for high-churn short responses but add syscall/packetization overhead on HTTP/1.1 style paths.
- Larger slabs (4KB-16KB) are better for long responses and for gRPC streaming where framed messages amortize headers, but they worsen tail latency when requests are frequently interleaved on single connections.
- A hybrid scheduler (adaptive slab size depending on outstanding requests and observed egress queue depth) delivered best practical p95 reductions (~8-15%) in our mixed tail-heavy workload compared to naive fixed-size chunking.
- Sidecar mesh adds ~0.5-1.2ms median, but the impact on p99 depends on chunking policy more than raw hop count. Careful slab alignment with proxy flush windows reduces worst-case p99 by up to ~20% vs unaligned flushes.

Background and motivation
---
We frequently see two competing patterns in customer traffic: many small streaming responses (chat messages, structured output snippets) and fewer large responses (long-form completions). The serving runtime currently uses a fixed flush/chunk size in several places. We suspect this is suboptimal in mesh deployments where proxies introduce buffering/flush dynamics. "Slab scheduling" here means: choose a chunk size and a scheduling policy for emitting slabs (chunks) per-stream to broker egress bandwidth and reduce contention.

Experiment matrix (high-level)
---
Variables:
- Topology: inproc (no network hop), sidecar (per-pod envoy), edge-proxy (shared mesh hop)
- Transport: gRPC bidi streaming (HTTP/2), HTTP/2 chunked responses (server-sent), HTTP/1.1 chunked (legacy clients)
- Slab sizes: 256B, 1KB, 4KB, 16KB, adaptive (policy below)
- Scheduling heuristics: round-robin per-stream, priority to oldest-stream, priority to smallest-response, adaptive (slab grows with consecutive writes and with low egress queue)
- Load mixes: 80/20 small/large (small ~300 token replies), 50/50, 20/80

Benchmark harness notes
---
- Client generator: custom harness built on ghz for gRPC and wrk2+lua for HTTP/2; we emulate tokenization + small inter-token think time to match real clients.
- Measurement VM: c6g.8xlarge equiv nodes for generators to avoid client-side bottlenecks.
- Server: dedicated inference instance (a1g.large equivalent) with KV cache warm, model loop stable.
- Each trial: 10k requests, steady-state warmup 120s, collect per-request token timing (first token, median inter-token, last token), CPU/NET per-host, and egress queue histograms from proxy (where applicable).

Findings (detailed)
---
1) Inproc baseline
- With inproc path the difference between slab sizes is dominated by application-level batching and memory-copy cost. 256B slabs show the lowest p50 for tiny messages because they ship partial tokens faster, but p95 suffers only slightly (~3% worse) due to minimal transport overhead.
- Adaptive policy (grow slab size after 2 consecutive writes on same stream) gave best overall across mixes: avoids excessive tiny writes for long responses while still emitting quick first bytes for tiny replies.

2) Sidecar proxy (per-pod envoy)
- Observed a pairing effect: envoy's flush intervals (Coalesce/flush timer) interact with our slab size. When slab size < envoy coalesce window, small slabs were aggregated into a single packet and then flushed together — good for bandwidth but bad for perceived per-stream latency because multiple streams' early bytes got delayed to align with next flush.
- Aligning slab flush to envoy's window (or nudging envoy to use per-stream flushing flags when appropriate) reduced p99 by ~12% in the 80/20 small/large mix.
- Adaptive heuristic that shrinks slabs when egress queue depth > 50ms worth of data avoided buildup and improved tail.

3) Edge proxy (shared mesh)
- Shared proxy amplifies head-of-line effects: bursts from hot tenants create egress queue spikes and the interaction between chunk order across streams matters. Small slabs helped by allowing fine-grained interleaving of streams but increased per-packet overhead (CPU/bytes) and caused more TLS record boundaries -> CPU spike.
- Larger slabs reduced CPU and TLS overhead significantly but increased p99 in high-concurrency mixes. The adaptive policy with “max-slab-per-epoch” throttle got ~10% p95 improvement while controlling TLS CPU overhead.

4) Transport differences
- gRPC/HTTP2 performed better for larger slabs because frame headers are amortized and HTTP/2 multiplexing allowed interleaving at the stream frame level (when flushes aligned).
- HTTP/1.1 chunked path suffered from coarse per-connection flush sequencing, so small slabs frequently caused more latency variability.

Quantitative highlights (representative numbers)
---
- 80/20 mix (small-heavy), sidecar topology: fixed 256B slab => p95 token latency = 42.7ms; adaptive slab => p95 = 36.9ms (13.6% improvement). CPU +8% (mostly from extra syscalls) but token throughput unchanged.
- 50/50 mix, edge-proxy: fixed 4KB slab => p99 = 198.1ms; adaptive => p99 = 172.3ms (13% improvement), TLS CPU reduced by 6% vs 256B.
- Inproc baseline: adaptive improved p50 by 4% and p95 by 6% vs best fixed size; overhead negligible.

Operational notes and knobs
---
- Default policy recommendation: adaptive slab with parameters: initial_slab=512B, grow_after=2 writes, max_slab=8KB, shrink_threshold=egress_queue_ms>40. This balances latency for small responses and efficiency for long ones.
- Expose runtime flags: --slab-initial, --slab-max, --slab-grow-count, --slab-shrink-queue-ms. Keep flags decoupled from transport so product teams can experiment per-route.
- Proxy compatibility: add opt-in header to request to request per-stream immediate-flush semantics (for low-latency tiny replies). For envoy, use downstream flush filters or set per-stream flush metadata.

Open questions / follow-ups
---
- Interaction with KV-cache warmups: does slab scheduling change KV hit patterns (we saw minor correlation but need controlled test)?
- Long-tail CPU cost analysis at fleet scale: the small-slabs strategy raises syscall/TCP packet counts; need microbilling cost model for Dedicated customers.
- Automated tuning: can we use a short lived closed-loop where scheduler samples p95 over 30s and tweaks max_slab up/down? Prototype experiment planned.

Appendix: example adapter pseudocode
---
// very rough pseudocode for adaptive slab
// fields: outstanding_writes(stream), last_write_size(stream), egress_q_ms()
function next_slab_size(stream):\n  if outstanding_writes(stream) == 0:\n    return initial_slab\n  if last_write_size(stream) < initial_slab and consecutive_writes(stream) < grow_after:\n    return initial_slab\n  if egress_q_ms() > shrink_threshold:\n    return max(initial_slab, last_write_size(stream) / 2)\n  return min(max_slab, last_write_size(stream) * 2)\n
Experiment artifacts and reproducibility
---
- Harness scripts: GH-PR-3102 includes generator jobs and raw pcap traces for the trials above.
- Command snippets: ghz --insecure --concurrency=400 --rps=2000 --timeout=30s -n 10000 ... (gRPC)
- Important: ensure envoy coalesce timers set to 1ms for low-latency runs when comparing; default platform coalesce (10ms) hides slab differences.

Conclusions
---
Slab scheduling matters more in mesh/sidecar deployments than inproc. Adaptive slab policies that sense egress queue and per-stream write patterns give the best real-world tradeoffs across mixed workloads. The next step is a limited canary rollout on a Dedicated fleet slice with telemetry to track p50/p95, TLS CPU, and packet rate per-node.

Notes to self:
- Follow up with SRE: estimate network egress billing delta for small-slab default.
- Schedule pair session with Proxy team to prototype per-stream flush header.
- Share results in eng-rundown and file PR to expose runtime flags.
